transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

When there’s a line or a process, I just can’t seem to wait my turn without jumping ahead or changing plans, and it keeps messing up our money and appointments. It’s gotten so bad that my family is at risk of falling behind on rent, and I just don't know how to stop myself.
Did you experience these difficulties with waiting your turn, impulsivity, or staying focused consistently since you were a child, or did these behaviors develop later in your life?

Yes, I've definitely had these struggles since I was a kid. Even back in elementary school, my teachers were always calling my mom because I couldn't stay in my seat, kept blurting things out, and got sent to the hallway for moving around and talking too much.
In addition to these impulsive behaviors, do you also frequently struggle with staying organized, losing necessary items, or failing to finish tasks you've started?

Yes, I really struggle with those. When I try to plan my week, I just get completely lost and end up missing deadlines or doing things in a panic at the very last minute. And if I try to run errands or do chores, I get sidetracked so easily that I leave them half-done, even though I really meant to finish them.

Would you say that your difficulties with staying focused and organized are just as problematic for you as the impulsive behaviors, or is the impulsivity and restlessness the main issue that causes trouble in your daily life?

Honestly, both are massive problems that work together to ruin my plans, just in different ways. The impulsivity and restlessness feel like immediate disasters when I jump ahead in lines or make snap decisions, but the focus and organization issues are just as damaging because drifting off and missing deadlines is what's putting our housing at risk.

latest_inference.note: The patient reports significant and persistent symptoms of both inattention (disorganization, losing items, failing to finish tasks) and hyperactivity/impulsivity (inability to wait, blurting out, restlessness) dating back to childhood. Because both symptom clusters are present and equally impairing, the diagnosis of the combined type is more appropriate than the predominantly inattentive or predominantly hyperactive types.
